en: The second [section], the verses spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai,
consists of one hundred and sixty-five lines and is divided into two parts:
the first one hundred lines are a verse summary of the preceding prose, while the latter sixty-five lines clarify the application of the sutra.
Regarding the method:
the preceding prose section contains both the opening analogy and the application of the analogy; the verse section likewise has two parts:
the first, consisting of sixty-five and a half lines, versifies the opening analogy.
Next, there are thirty-four and a half lines of verse that combine the illustrations with the meaning.
This section also has two parts:
first, there are thirty-three lines of verse that illustrate the general illustration; [the second part follows].
Next, there are thirty-two and a half verses that provide individual analogies.

These verses summarize six points of meaning; of these six, they explicitly praise four, while implicitly encompassing two. Specifically, the praise of the house also encompasses one gate, and the praise of the five hundred men also encompasses the thirty sons.
The first line clarifies the "Elder" (*śreṣṭhin*), which is a verse praising his title; it simultaneously extols both his name and his conduct.

Since he possesses the virtue of being a leader of men, we know that his reputation and conduct are universally revered throughout the kingdom and its towns; we also know that both his internal and external qualities, as well as his age and virtue, are preeminent. Internally, this corresponds to the *Bhagavat*, the title of the Buddha, signifying that he himself is fully endowed with wisdom, the severance of afflictions, compassion, and all myriad virtues.
"‘There was a great house’" and below—this second section consists of three lines and one phrase, which versifies the second simile of the household above. It is divided into two parts:
the first line versifies the vastness of the house;

"‘That house was long-standing and old’" and below—this second part consists of three lines that extensively set forth the substance of the house and clarify the characteristics of what is being burned; thus, it is known that this [section] versifies the substance of the house.
The three realms being beginningless constitutes "long-standing"; not having been created in the present constitutes "ancient"; and their impermanence and baseness are termed "sudden decay.
It is also said that the head is the upper chamber, the belly is the hall, and the back is the house; their moment-to-moment succession and impermanence constitute "perilous height."

One interpretation states that the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) is the "hall," while the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu) is the "house"; being unable to avoid falling from these is called "high danger. The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) supports them like a "pillar," and past karma constitutes the "foundation steps."
It is also said that the two feet are the "foundation pillar," while being subject to the three marks of existence is called "decaying and crumbling.
The governing framework of the mental consciousness serves as the "beams and rafters," and being destroyed by various sufferings is like "tilting and collapsing."
It is also said that the spinal vertebrae are the "beams and rafters," the ribs are the "foundation steps," and the time of old age and decay is the "collapse and ruin.

Regarding the "walls," one interpretation holds that the four great elements are the "walls," the skin is the "plaster," the improper conduct of the four postures is the "falling into disorder," and the dullness of the five consciousnesses, which do not govern their respective objects, is the "displacement and omission."

It is also said: "The crumbling of walls and foundations" refers to the skin becoming cracked and withered; the vigor of youth is fresh and pure like newly applied plaster, while the decrepitude of old age is parched and emaciated like later peeling and falling away. When hair and beard grow old and decay, they all fall out like "thatch tiles falling in disarray"; when the sinews and bones grow weak, the joints fail to support one another like "rafters and eaves falling apart."
Regarding the phrase "surrounded by enclosures and winding curves," the Seal Master (Yinshi) says:

"It is called 'surrounded by enclosures' because the thirty-six impure substances mutually obstruct one another; it is called 'winding curves' because they coil like pig intestines. Not only are they subject to the transience of impermanence, but they are also filled with impurity, suffering, and so forth; therefore, it is said that 'filth and impurities pervade them.'"

Now it is said that "surrounding obstructions" refers to the six consciousnesses, and "crookedness" refers to the six sense organs. Because the six consciousnesses take objects by depending on the six sense organs through a difficult and circuitous process, they are called "crooked. Because the six sense objects universally defile the six sense organs, it is said that "impurities are everywhere pervasive."
The two successive explanations regarding causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the contemplation of the mind (*citta-parīkṣā*), and so forth.
From "There were five hundred people" onwards is the third section; this half-line verse summarizes the third preceding point, the analogy of the five hundred people.
The faculties and natures of the three vehicles are subsumed within the five destinies; this also corresponds to the analogy of the thirty sons.
From the verse on "the owls" (*cī-cāo*) downward, the fourth section contains twenty-nine lines of verse, which directly eulogize the fifth section above, "The Arising of Fire."
This section further consists of four parts:
first, there are twenty-two verses clarifying the events on the ground, which serve as a metaphor for the fire breaking out in the desire realm;
next, there are three and a half verses clarifying the events within the hole, which serve as a metaphor for the fire breaking out in the form realm.
Next, three verses and a half clarify the matters within emptiness, using the analogy of fire arising in the formless realm;
finally, the fourth section consists of one verse, which summarizes that the various objections are not limited to a single point.
Regarding the arising of fire in the desire realm, there are further four sections:
first, seventeen and a half verses clarify the categories of things burned, which are analogous to the ten afflictions (*daśa-kleśa*) of sentient beings;
second, one and a half verses clarify the causes for the fire’s arising, which are analogous to the origins from which the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) arise.
The next third section, consisting of one and a half lines, clarifies the momentum of the fire’s arising, which is likened to the actual emergence of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).

The subsequent fourth section, also consisting of one and a half lines, clarifies the signs of being consumed by the flames, which is likened to undergoing the eight sufferings amidst the five turbidities.
Regarding the first [section], the seventeen lines and a half are further divided into two parts:
the first sixteen lines correctly clarify that which is burned;
the final one and a half lines provide a summary.
Within the section on those who are burned, there are further two parts:
the first six lines clarify that birds and beasts are burned, serving as a metaphor for sentient beings with the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mūrdha-kleśa*);
the subsequent ten lines clarify that ghosts and spirits are burned, serving as a metaphor for sentient beings with the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśa*).
The first five dull fetters (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*) are divided into two parts:
the first five lines and a half clarify the five dull [fetters],
and the second, half line, provides the conclusion.
Now, first, the five dull [defilements] constitute five [categories]:
the first half-verse is a simile for the latent tendency of pride (*māna-anuśaya*).
Sentient beings exalt themselves and look down upon others, just as the nature of a bird is to soar high and gaze downward.
The eight birds are a metaphor for the eight types of pride (*māna*); the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* clarifies the eight kinds of arrogance (*mada*), which are now correlated with these eight birds.

Arrogance of physical vigor is like the hawk; arrogance of temperament is like the owl; arrogance of wealth is like the eagle; arrogance of power is like the vulture; arrogance of longevity is like the crow; arrogance of intelligence is like the magpie; arrogance of virtuous conduct is like the pigeon; and arrogance of physical beauty is like the dove. To look down upon others is arrogance; to esteem oneself is arrogance. To cherish oneself is greed; to desire another is lust. To be angry with oneself is resentment; to be angry at another is hatred. To be deluded about oneself is folly; to delude another is ignorance, and so forth.
Next, following the section on "the venomous snake," the second part consists of two lines which illustrate the latent tendency of anger (*dveṣānuśaya*).
There are three types of anger:
the venom of a snake is so potent that it can be drawn in by inhalation even without being touched; this illustrates anger arising from irrationality (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
The viper and the scorpion sting when touched; this is likened to anger directed at [one who] upholds the Dharma.
The centipede is likened to anger arising from frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
People of the world say that those with red necks are centipedes, while those that are not red are millipedes.
Below "The Lizard" (shǒugōng), third, two lines: these illustrate the latent tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*).

Delusion arises both independently and in association. The lizard, the centipede, and the like, which are motionless, illustrate independent ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*); the langur, the wildcat, and the mouse illustrate [delusion] arising in association.
"Various evil insects" and below: from the root of delusion (*moha*), all fetters (*saṃyojana*) arise in full.

This clarifies the characteristics of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*): they condition one another, perhaps crisscrossing throughout the three realms, arising with a swiftness like that of a galloping horse.

The line following "feces and urine" clarifies that the objects to which the deluded mind clings are all impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure; because one fails to understand this due to delusion (*moha*), one conceives of them as pure and so forth, thereby giving rise to defiled attachment. Thus it says, "dung beetles and various insects gather upon them."
Below "Fox and Wolf," fourth, two lines, clarifying the latent tendency of greed (*rāga-anuśaya*).
There are two kinds of greed:
first, that which possesses power; second, that which lacks power.
Those with power take [what they need] by means of their authority and might, like foxes and wolves;
those without power can only beg from others for coarse and inferior things, like jackals.
Below, "chewing" clarifies the grasping for objects; it draws things toward oneself like "chewing," and does not employ reason, like "treading."
The greedy mind grasps objects, whether seizing a single city or an entire kingdom; its boundaries are like those of "gnawing.

It is also said that the greedy mind grasps objects with or without utility: grasping what is useful is like "chewing," while grasping what is useless is like "treading upon"; furthermore, when the amount is small it is "chewing," and when it is large it is "treading upon."
"Bone and flesh strewn in disarray" refers to the accumulation of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) without knowing moderation or contentment.
"Thereupon, a pack of dogs comes vying to seize and tear them apart" refers to powerful greed (*rāga*), which seizes and tears apart those who are powerless—namely, kings and thieves.

"Starving, emaciated, and terrified" means that one is like a hungry person who is never satisfied; one is like an emaciated person whose seeking yields nothing; and one is like a terrified person in constant pursuit. Such a person of excessive desire is poor despite being wealthy.
The mind of affectionate love craves the flesh of the five sensory objects;

the mind of views craves the bones of principles. As one pursues knowledge and views, what is understood becomes manifold—this is like having many bones—and dogs craving bone vie with one another to seize them.

Among those with various views, not having obtained the food of the True Dharma is called hunger; being unable to subdue and sever these views is called debility; and seeking understanding everywhere is called panic.
One interpretation states that this refers to the longing and expectations of a greedy person.
"Quarreling and seizing" constitutes the fifth section; these two phrases serve as a metaphor for the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*).

Hesitation between two extremes is called doubt (*vicikitsā*); when one has not yet decided whether something is right or wrong, there arises contention. To think "this is correct" is called *che*, while to think "this is incorrect" is called *cha*.
"Barking and howling" refers to the utterance of speech to decide upon the principles of right and wrong.
The two lines beginning with "Terror" constitute the second section, which concludes the discussion on the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*).
The section beginning with "In every place" contains ten lines and constitutes the second [major] division, clarifying the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśa*).
This consists of two parts:

the first half-line provides a general explanation of the sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*), as these sharp faculties universally take the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the four truths (*catuḥ-satya*) as their objects; therefore, it says "they exist everywhere."

Now, ghosts and spirits possess both penetration and wisdom, whereas birds and beasts do not; therefore, the "sharp" afflictions (kleśas) are used as an analogy for ghosts and spirits, while the "dull" afflictions are likened to insects and beasts.
Below the term "yakṣa," the second section—consisting of nine lines and a half—specifically elucidates the five sharp afflictions.
It consists of five parts:

the first three lines clarify the yakṣa, who is a swift-moving spirit; this is a metaphor for those with false views who deny cause and effect. "Human" represents the retribution of goodness, which is a metaphor for supramundane cause and effect that is untainted by afflictions.
To deny this principle is like eating human flesh.

The category of venomous insects represents an evil retribution; just as in the world there are causes and effects mixed with various afflictions, to deny this principle is like consuming venomous insects.
"Conception, gestation, and birth" refers to the worldly phenomenon wherein a cause of its own kind produces an effect of its own kind.

"Each concealing and protecting itself": because the cause possesses the potential for the effect, it is called "concealing"; because the effect will certainly be obtained without being lost, it is called "protecting."
Furthermore, human flesh is good and poisonous insects are evil; yet with a mind of false view, one denies the causality of good and evil, treating the matter as if it were merely a case of eating.
The phrase "incubating, nursing, giving birth, and producing" generally describes how both good and evil possess the functional capacity for causes and effects to arise from one another.
"Having eaten his fill" refers to the accomplishment of the mind of views.
"The evil mind blazes intensely" refers to the expansion of the mind of views.

"The sound of strife" means that while the internal mind is accomplished, it manifests externally through verbal teaching, proclaiming a doctrine of no cause and no effect that causes those who hear it to fall into the three miserable realms; therefore, it is called "terror."
Below "Kumbhāṇḍa," the second section consists of two lines and two phrases, which serve as a metaphor for the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Kumbhāṇṇḍas are superior among ghosts; likewise, tainted wholesome states (*sāsrava-kuśala*) are capable of overcoming various insects.

Regarding "squatting on a mound of earth": practicing the ten wholesome precepts can lead to rebirth in the six heavens; these six heavens are the high places within the desire realm, and their nature is like that of a mound of earth.

Furthermore, when non-Buddhists maintain the precepts and are able to cultivate meditative concentration, they may initially attain the concentration of the desire realm, or they may attain the "preparatory" (anāgamya) concentration. This preparatory concentration has not yet transcended the desire realm; its summit is like a mound of earth.

Regarding the phrase "or separated by one or two chi": attaining the concentration of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-samādhi*) is like being at a distance of one chi; attaining the concentration of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-samādhi*) is like being at a distance of two chi. Attaining rebirth in a higher realm is "going," while falling back and descending is "returning. Giving rise to the hindrance of views (*dṛṣṭi-nīvaraṇa*) is like "indulging in idle play."

Regarding "seizing the two paws of the dog": one explanation states that slandering the absence of the cause of suffering is like seizing the dog's paws; repudiating the absence of the fruit of suffering is like placing its feet around its neck; and the fundamental accumulation that results in the attainment of the fruit is like the dog's bark. When those with sharp insight proclaim that there is no principle of accumulation or the attainment of suffering, it causes the dog to lose its voice.
Regarding "contemplative understanding," one cultivates the contemplation of the six aspects to subdue greed; when greed does not arise, it appears as if it has been severed, like a loss of voice.

The dog represents sensual greed (*kāmarāga*); the two legs represent applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). As these thoughts come and go, they are constantly present within the sphere of greed. Counting the breaths to still the mind carries the meaning of binding, for it serves to capture the applied and sustained thoughts.

"Striking" refers to when a craving-thought is strong and turns toward an impure object; one then applies the contemplation of impurity to subdue that craving-thought. Once the craving-thought is crushed and subdued, it is like a dog being struck that is unable to bark.
It is further said: "Practicing the contemplation of impurity is like striking a dog; being able to generate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is like the dog losing its voice upon being struck.
Regarding "placing the foot upon the neck": although the dog may be struck, it stirs and does not submit, so one further places a foot upon it.

Although greed may know that it is impure and cease for a time, greed is still not entirely stilled; therefore, one further applies the contemplation of impermanence as a "foot" to strike at the "neck" of clinging to permanence. Thus, fear arises and the thought of greed no longer emerges.
Furthermore, it is said: "First, restraining the mind is like throwing oneself toward the ground;
constantly binding it to its object is like placing a foot upon the neck so that one cannot rise.

Regarding "fearing the dog while enjoying oneself," this means using the cultivation of the awareness of impermanence to awaken from greed, which is like fearing the dog; because of this, one attains the flavor of dhyāna, which is called "enjoying oneself."
From "His body is tall and large" onwards is the third section, consisting of one and a half verses, which uses a metaphor for the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi).

Calculating a self by extending it through the three periods of time is called "tall"; calculating a self as pervading the five aggregates horizontally is called "large. Because one calculates a self as autonomous and fails to cultivate wholesome dharmas, one lacks shame and remorse, and is thus said to be "naked. Because one is adorned with evil, one is said to be "black. Because one lacks the provisions of merit, one is said to be "emaciated."
Since those who conceive of a self do not transcend the triple world, it is said that they "constantly dwell therein.
Because they conceive of a self within the mind and utter speech proclaiming the characteristics of a self, it is said that they "emit a great evil sound."
"Because they hope to attain the fruits of the Path by means of this teaching, it is said that they 'cry out seeking food.
From "Furthermore, there are various ghosts" onwards is the fourth section; the half-line illustrates the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

Their throats are as narrow as needles yet they preserve their lives; they perceive the non-perception realm as permanent and calculate it to be nirvana. Therefore, it says, "their throats are like needles.
The section beginning with "heads like oxen" is the fifth part, consisting of two lines, which serves as a metaphor for extreme views (antagrāhadṛṣṭi).

To speculate on the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism is like the two horns on a cow’s head; whether one holds that "the body is the self" or "the self is the body," these views of extremes arise based on the view of a self, just like the two horns on a head.
To calculate the faults of eternalism and nihilism, they are able to sever supramundane goodness, like eating human flesh;
they are able to sever mundane roots of goodness, like "sometimes eating dog."
Sometimes they calculate permanence, and sometimes they calculate annihilation; their shifting back and forth is like "disheveled hair.
Calculating permanence destroys the notion of annihilation, while calculating annihilation destroys the notion of permanence, like "cruel and violent harm."
Lacking the food and drink of wisdom and meditative concentration for self-sustenance, they are "oppressed by hunger and thirst.

From the passage beginning with "yakṣas and hungry ghosts" below, the second section—consisting of one and a half lines—summarizes the characteristics of afflictions in the desire realm; it also concludes the characteristics of beings who are purely [afflicted], all of whom possess outflowing (sāsrava) minds that constantly lack the flavor of the Path, and are therefore said to be "in urgent hunger."

"Peering through a window" means that although one observes the principle of emptiness and yearns for the flavor of the Way, one remains attached despite such observation; the mind frequently fails to accord with the true principle, just as one who peers through a window at the sky cannot perceive it without obstruction.
"‘This dilapidated old house belongs to one person’" marks the second section, consisting of one verse, which clarifies the cause of the fire.

The triple world is the realm where the Buddha manifests his transformation; since he has resolved to attain enlightenment, he has vowed to deliver all beings from it, and thus it is said to "belong to one person."

The elder was able to ensure that his house was protected from fire; however, after he had departed, because his sons were ignorant, the fire broke out. This corresponds internally to the fact that during the time of the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, he constantly taught these beings to subdue the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*). When the conditions for the Tathāgata’s manifestation were exhausted, he relinquished his response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*); yet these beings subsequently gave rise to the five corruptions. Since he went to other lands to respond to their conditions rather than departing forever, it is said that "he has recently gone out."

Furthermore, it is said that from the moment one attains non-arising (*anutpāda*), one no longer takes birth within the triple world; thus, it is called "exiting. Because one will soon come [to manifest], it is called "near.
The *Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta* states, "He frequently manifests nirvāṇa," which is precisely the intention behind "leaving the house."
Below the phrase "in the later residence," the third section consists of two lines that correctly elucidates the momentum of the fire's outbreak.

"In all four directions" refers to the locus; because the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena give rise to the four inversions, the five turbidities, and the eight sufferings, it is called "simultaneously. Their continuous and gradual increase is "blazing"; the severing of the life-faculty is "cracking"; and the disintegration of the body by the wind-blade is "rending."

Furthermore, it is said that the sounds of groaning and lamentation while undergoing suffering are called "cracking"; the destruction of the sense faculties is called "splitting"; the severing of breath, the separation of bones, and the snapping of tendons are called "breaking and falling"; and the dissolution of the four great elements is called "the collapsing of walls."
"Various ghosts and spirits," etc., is the fourth section; one and a half lines clarify the signs of being burned.

Some say that "ghosts and spirits" refers to relatives and "raising one's voice" refers to weeping; however, following the previous analogy with the sharp-faculties (li-shi), this is used here as a metaphor for deities and demons.

Those who possess sharp faculties may speculate on either eternalism or annihilationism. If they speculate on eternalism, they claim that the nature of dharmas is definitively empty: what already exists returns to non-existence, and this non-existence is precisely eternity.

Those who speculate on annihilationism claim that the nature of dharmas is definitively annihilated: there is only this single death, with no further continuation. Both groups proclaim their definitive assertions, stating that the matter has already been made manifest; thus it is said, "raising their voices in a great cry."

If they are those with dull afflictions and various forms of attachment to precepts and rituals, they originally did not intend to sever [the fetters]; now, seeing impermanence, they merely give rise to doubt and fear, not knowing the means for deliverance. Therefore, it is said: "They are terrified and unable to escape on their own."

Below the phrase “malicious beasts and venomous insects,” the second section, spanning three lines and a half, clarifies the matters within the cave, serving as an analogy for the outbreak of fire in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). This is the very passage where various schools interpret the meaning of "hatred" (*dveṣa*) as pervading all three realms.
The text consists of four parts.
The first line clarifies the categories of things that are burned.

The meditative concentration of the four dhyānas is like a hollow space; although it does not reach the open expanse outside the gate, it can still escape the fierce flames, and by entering into dhyāna-concentration, one can likewise escape the coarse evils of the desire realm.
Benefiting sentient beings so that they too may attain meditative concentration, even the piśāca demons dwell therein.
The phrase "because of meager merit" is the second [point], the cause for the fire’s outbreak; because their merit is slight, they draw near to evil and encounter suffering.

The phrase "oppressed by fire" is the third point, clarifying the momentum of the fire's arising: although there is no fierce flame within the hollows, there is still the affliction of heat; likewise, although the fourth dhyāna lacks the evils of the desire realm, it still possesses the subtle suffering of attachment to its flavors. Therefore, it is said to be "oppressed by fire."

Below the phrase "mutually harming one another," the fourth section consists of two lines which clarify the signs of being burned and the signs of the sharp and the dull competing for superiority. It explains that while all sentient beings who attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are the same in this regard, their respective conceptualizations differ; because these differ, they mutually affirm and negate one another, just as they harm each other.

Once one gives rise to various views within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one can no longer produce untainted (*anāsrava*) concentration and wisdom; instead, one merely clings to silence, which is like "drinking blood," and clings to the five factors [of the dhyānas], which is like "eating meat. The "jackal" represents the greed of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), which has already been severed by the attainment of the *anāgāmi* stage; thus it is said that they have "already died beforehand. This is also called "devouring," for the greed for meditative concentration is like a great predatory beast capable of swallowing the greed of the desire realm.

The four inversions and eight sufferings of the desire realm are like "fierce flames," while the four inversions of the form realm and these sufferings are like "stinking smoke. Since these also pervade the body, sensations, mind, dharmas, the four great elements, skin, flesh, and so forth, it is said that they "fill and obstruct all four directions."
Below the section on the centipede, third, two and a half verses clarify the phenomena within emptiness, serving as a metaphor for the arising of fire in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This is divided into two parts:
the first verse clarifies the categories of things that are burned; [the remainder clarifies the nature of the burning].
The subsequent one and a half lines clarify the characteristics of that which is burned.

One who is weary of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) emerges from it and turns toward the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); being weary of the coarse objects of form, they contemplate the dharmas of the formless realm. This is like a venomous snake emerging from its hole due to being scorched by fire; if this is so, then hatred (*dveṣa*) pervades all three realms.
If one attains the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*), one must necessarily extinguish the objects of lower realms; hence it is said, "taking whatever is available as food.

Even at the highest peak, the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one still cannot escape the various sufferings of perversion, which are like "a fire burning upon the head."
The realm of non-perception likewise possesses the fires of the eight sufferings:
the arising of divergent thoughts in the mind is called the suffering of birth;
the non-abiding of every momentary thought is called the suffering of aging.
A mind that is distracted and agitated during practice hinders meditative concentration and is called the suffering of illness;
the regression from concentration is the suffering of death;
and failing to attain concentration despite seeking it is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
If one seeks meditative concentration and fails to attain it, there must be an obstruction; this is precisely the suffering of association with the loathed (*pratigha-saṃyoga-duḥkha*).
The mind consisting of the four aggregates is the suffering of the five burgeoning aggregates (*pañca-skandha-duḥkha*).
Because one cannot immediately sever the seeds of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the fire burns upon one's head.
Because they lack the untainted [state], they are tormented by hunger and thirst; this is still the frantic wandering and distress of saṃsāra.

From the words "The house is like this" onwards is the fourth section, one line in length, which summarizes that the various hardships within the three realms are not limited to one; thus concludes the general analogy.
"Below the phrase 'At that time, the householder stood outside the gate,' there are thirty-two and a half verses praising the second specific parable.
There are four specific parables, yet here only three are praised."
The first section consists of two and a half lines, which eulogize the elder seeing the fire;
the second section consists of thirteen lines, which eulogize the abandonment of the small bench for the carriage and the analogy of giving the great to the large and the small to the small;
the third section consists of seventeen lines, which eulogize the bestowal of the great carriages.
The first two and a half verses describe the perception of fire, which has three aspects:
first, the perceiver; second, the perceived object; and third, the arising of alarm and fear; these are all fully contained within these verses.

The first three phrases, beginning with "the master of the house," refer to the person who perceives; whereas the preceding section clarified "seeing," here it says "hearing," substituting hearing for seeing, as hearing necessarily derives from another.
“Standing outside the gate” is a direct verse praising the aforementioned fact that although I am able to emerge safely from the burning gate,

“standing” means that while abiding in the stage of the Dharmakāya, one constantly harbors great compassion, desiring to save sentient beings and thus does not remain seated upon the throne of ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
The old [commentary] says: The Buddhas of the ten directions said to Śākyamuni, "Your karmically connected children are within the triple world, and their roots of goodness are about to perish.
It further states: "The capacity of sentient beings to respond to the Buddha is for the sake of others."
Now it is said that "the Dharma is the Teacher of the Buddha," referring to the dharma of samādhi; when this dharma acts as the teacher, it is "another person.
If one enters samādhi, one can perceive the capacities [of sentient beings]; since samādhi enables the Buddha to see, it is said, "there is someone who says."
It further states: "Great Compassion is another person," and so forth.
From the words "You, my sons," etc., the second section—consisting of one line and one phrase—versifies the fire that is perceived.
Question:
Since the child was originally not yet born, how did he enter through play?
Answer:
Alternatively, having once resolved to attain enlightenment, one is said to have "exited" the triple world; yet to subsequently regress is called "entering.
This is like a person who raises their foot intending to leave through a gate, but turns back instead; they are thus said both to have exited and to have returned and entered.

Furthermore, the nature of reality is fundamentally pure and is not a phenomenon of the triple world; yet, due to ignorance, conceptual proliferation arises, whereby birth and death ensue. Therefore, it is said: "First, because of playful activity, one enters [into this state]."
The fact that great goodness has not yet taken root is termed "infantile," and being shrouded by ignorance is termed "ignorant.

From the line "Having heard this, they were startled and entered [the path]" onwards, the third section consists of two lines; these verses summarize the aforementioned state of being greatly terrified and the subsequent arousal of the mind of great compassion.

Below the phrase "it is appropriate to provide relief," the second section consists of thirteen lines. This praises the abandonment of the small table and the use of the carriage, which is divided into two parts. The first part, comprising five and a half lines, praises the failure to save the child mentioned above.

In the preceding section, both exhortation and admonition were presented within the parable; in the subsequent section, only the exhortation was correlated. Now, only the admonition is being versified.
There are three parts to the text of the admonition, and here too there are three:
the first four and a half verses versify the preceding passage on "I shall speak of the terrors" as a proposal of suitability.
Next, from "The sons were ignorant" onwards, the second section consists of three lines, which eulogize the failure to accept the admonitions;
"They continued their play without ceasing," the third section consists of one line, which directly eulogizes the cessation of the transformative teaching.
"Appropriate means" (*fangyi*) refers to preparing for the Great Teaching.
"Informing and exhorting" (*gaoyu*) signifies the sense of preaching and admonishing regarding various afflictions and hardships.
The phrase "not yet finished" (*biji*) is a verse summarizing the meaning of the preceding line, "regarding his father," which conveys the sense of casting aside words of suffering.
"Then the elder had this thought," and so forth; the second section consists of seven and a half stanzas praising the use of the carts.
This section has four parts:
first, the preparation of the three carts.
Second, knowing the sons' prior thoughts;
third, praising the rarity of the three vehicles;
fourth, fulfilling the sons' wishes.
Now, this verse contains only three meanings; it briefly omits the praise of knowing the sons' prior thoughts.

The first three lines constitute the preliminary adaptation, while the second part—consisting of three verses beginning with "Addressing all the sons"—is an exhortation and praise for the rarity of the three vehicles.

The preceding section clarified the three meanings of exhortation (*anuśāsanī*), demonstration (*darśana*), and realization (*sākṣātkriyā*); now, this verse also contains these three meanings. Re-verse the exhortation to form four parts:
first, one line of verse exhorting;
next, from "the sheep-cart" downward, the second part, with three lines of verse demonstrating; [and so forth].
Next, "Come forth, you all," is the third section, a single line that further praises the exhortation;
next, from "I shall act for your sake" onwards, is the fourth section, a single verse that praises the testimony.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Hearing it said that there are such chariots," this third section, consisting of one and a half verses, praises the wishes of the sons.
Here, the preceding six lines are summarized as a whole: "galloping" praises the realization of the Truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*), and "open ground" praises the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

From "The elder sees his children emerge from the burning house" onwards, the third section consists of seventeen verses, which eulogize the preceding parable of the equal bestowal of the great carts.
The preceding passage consists of four parts:
first, escaping the peril; second, requesting the vehicle; third, being equally granted the great vehicle; and fourth, rejoicing upon obtaining the vehicle.
Now, this verse also has four parts:
The first five lines of verse describe the joy of being freed from danger;

the second, three lines, describe the request for the vehicle; the third, seven and a half lines, describe the equal bestowal; and the fourth, one and a half lines, describes the joy of obtaining the vehicle.
Regarding the first five verses on how the sons were spared from calamity, there are two parts:
first, one verse praising their escape from danger;
second, the following four verses beginning with "And themselves," praising their joy.
Regarding the phrase "sitting upon the lion throne," there are two interpretations.
First, it is said that when the sons sit upon the throne, they have escaped the three realms and are therefore fearless.

Second, it is said that this refers to the elder sitting upon the throne; having seen his sons escape the calamity, the elder immediately attains fearlessness. Previously, while still outside the gate, he was still subject to anxiety and fear, which is why it is said he was "standing"; now that they have emerged from the gate, he finally sits in fearlessness. Thus, the *Upāya-paryāya-parivarta* (Chapter on Expedient Means) states: "Now I am joyful and fearless."
The "Text on Avoiding Calamities" concludes.
From the phrase "and rejoiced in himself" onwards, the second section consists of four lines, praising the elder’s joy as described in the prose.
From the phrase "knowing his father was sitting at ease" onwards, the second section consists of three lines of verse, praising the second request for a vehicle, as described in the prose.

From "The elder is immensely wealthy" onwards is the third section, consisting of seven and a half lines. It versifies the third point above, the equal bestowal of the great chariots. The preceding prose contains two chapters, two extensive expositions, and two explanations, totaling five textual units; here, however, only four are versified, as the extensive exposition of the [father's] mind and the explanation of the [sons'] mind are not versified.

The first line [of the verse] skips over the fourth [verse] to explain the "Great Vehicle" (*mahāyāna*). A house that contains things is called a "storehouse" (*kośa*), while the ground that contains them is called a "treasury" (*nidhi*); because it possesses all dharmas, the practice is called a "treasury," and because the six faculties—eye, ear, and so forth—possess all dharmas, they are called "storehouses," and so on.
"Next, with various precious objects," and so forth, constitutes the second section: six lines of verse praising the third [gift], the Great Carriage.
The first two lines praise two thematic headings; the line "With these wonderful carriages" constitutes the third, praising the second thematic heading, the Great Carriage.
The phrase "equally bestowing upon all sons" is the fourth [section], which versifies the introductory chapter on the impartial mind.

The passage beginning with "At that time, all the sons were filled with joy and leaped for gladness," consisting of one and a half lines, is the fourth [section], which versifies the joy of receiving the chariots.

"Roaming in the four directions" means that, riding upon the wisdom of the Middle Way, one traverses horizontally through the fourfold sets of four gates and the fourfold sets of the Four Noble Truths, and traverses vertically through the forty-one stages and the ultimate virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; therefore, it is said that one sports with sovereign ease.
"Tell Śāriputra that I am also like this," and so forth; the second section, consisting of thirty-four and a half lines, constitutes the verses that correlate with the parables.
The first four lines correlate with the general parable as a whole, employing four points of meaning which simultaneously encompass six parables.

The single line "I am also like this" correlates with the Elder; the first half of the verse correlates with his title and rank, while the second half correlates with his name, conduct, and the meaning of praising his virtues.
The one honored among the worthy and noble through seven kinds of skillful means, and the father of the world through nine kinds.
The single verse, "All sentient beings are my children," encompasses the five paths of rebirth and carries a meaning that includes the thirty children.
The thirty sons are the causal factors, while all sentient beings are the primary factors.
The half-verse, "There is no peace in the three realms," praises the entire household and simultaneously conveys the meaning of the single gate.
The one and a half verses beginning with "Filled with manifold sufferings" summarize the analogy of the fire breaking out;
this concludes the summary of the general analogy.
From the passage "The Tathāgata has already left the burning house of the triple world" onwards, for thirty and a half lines, is the second section: the summary of the specific analogies.
The preceding verse opened with the statement that there is nothing that is not empty; this present verse combines [the two] to show that there is indeed [a conventional existence].
The first three verses of the commentary illustrate how seeing all sentient beings subject to birth, old age, and so forth is analogous to seeing a fire.
The preceding verse concerning the analogy of fire consists of three parts; now, this [section] also consists of three:

first, one verse praises the Tathāgata’s ability to see—specifically, that it is precisely because he dwells in tranquil seclusion that he can see the sons amidst the five turbidities—which corresponds to hearing someone say;

next, from "Now, in these three realms" onwards, the second part, consisting of one and a half lines, praises those sentient beings seen above who are being scorched and boiled by birth, old age, sickness, and death, corresponding to the second analogy of fire seen.

"Only I alone," and so forth: the third section, consisting of half a verse, praises the aforementioned passage where the Buddha, having perceived this, thought thus and was moved with alarm to enter the burning house.

"Although he further instructs and admonishes," and so forth, is the second section; these four lines of verse illustrate the analogy of discarding the small table and using the carriage. It is divided into two parts:
the first line illustrates the discarding of the small table and so forth.

The preceding section on analogies contained three points: the suitability [of the teaching], the lack of receptive capacity (*anadhikāra*), and the cessation of transformation. Now, this single verse also contains these three meanings, though they are presented in a general and abbreviated manner.

The phrase "although he instructs and admonishes" eulogizes the suitability; the phrase "yet they do not believe or accept it" eulogizes the lack of receptive capacity; and the final two lines eulogize the cessation of transformation.
Alternatively, the final two lines may be understood as eulogizing the lack of receptive capacity.
"Because their attachment is deep" refers to the fact that, as mentioned above, they have not yet escaped birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction.

From "By these skillful means" onwards is the second section, consisting of three verses, which versify the parable of using a vehicle to rescue the children. While the preceding prose contains four points, here only three are versified; likewise, there are only three in the summary, as the point regarding knowing the children's previous inclinations is omitted from the summary.
First, the single phrase "By these skillful means" eulogizes the preceding [verse] on merely employing wisdom and skillful means according to what is appropriate.
Second, from "He preaches the three vehicles" downward, one line and one phrase, eulogize the third [section] above, which praises the rarity of the three carts.
Third, from "These sons" downward, one and a half lines, eulogize the fourth [section], which accords with their wishes.
Above, each of the three vehicles was treated with four phrases; now, they are summarized in verse.

"If the mind is resolute" refers to that which is above the stage of patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*); this single phrase summarizes the stage of "running toward" for all three vehicles.
The subsequent line, beginning with "endowed with," summarizes the stage of "striving to emerge" for each of the three vehicles respectively.
"O Śāriputra, for you... and so forth; this third section consists of eight lines of verse, which correspond to the third [section] of the prose, the parable of bestowing the great chariots equally.
While the prose does not include the seeking of the chariots or the expression of joy, the verses reveal these elements in their entirety.

The verse now summarizes the equal bestowal and the joy; it does not summarize the avoidance of calamity or the request for a vehicle. There are two parts in total: the first five lines summarize the equal bestowal, and the latter three lines summarize the joy.
Regarding the four superior gifts previously bestowed, two were not versified; now, these are further condensed, combining only the two chapter-headings and the third, the "Vast Vehicle.

Furthermore, the verse explains the reason for the existence of this vehicle: the first line, beginning with "Your śarīra," first versifies the chapter-heading of the Great Vehicle, which refers to the various Buddhas’ meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and so forth mentioned in the preceding prose.

Next, from "If you all can... onwards is the second section, a single line of verse summarizing the chapter on the Equal Mind; the preceding text stated that these sentient beings are those who have escaped the three realms.

Next, from "This vehicle is subtle and wondrous" onwards is the third section; these two lines of verse synthesize the correct and vast carriage. The preceding passage states that "all are of one characteristic and one kind," and so forth. Next, from "Immeasurable billions of powers and liberations" onwards is the fourth section; this single line of verse explains the reason for the existence of the carriage mentioned above.
"Obtaining such a vehicle" and below constitutes the second section, consisting of three verses, which praise the joy of obtaining the vehicles.
This section is further divided into two parts:
the first two verses clarify that each has obtained a great vehicle;
Below the section beginning with "For this reason," the second part consists of one verse that concludes by exhorting faith.

Now, regarding the first two verses: "Day and night" means that when one first attains the Middle Way wisdom-light of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, it is like the division of day; ignorance remaining is like the night.
When one personally attains Middle Way wisdom, it is like day; entering birth-and-death through compassion is like night.
Because they constantly practice two dharmas, it is said that they "sport.
Since those of the three vehicles equally enter the Buddha's wisdom, it says, "together with all bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas."
Furthermore, this explains both self-cultivation and the transformation of others: because one attains this vehicle through self-cultivation, it is said that "one sports day and night";
because one uses this to transform others, it is said "together with the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas."
Being able to transform beings through the three vehicles is what is meant by "riding together on the precious vehicle.

The next verse explains that there are no causes or conditions for a third vehicle; having investigated and sought throughout the lands of the ten directions, one finds that it is truly and exclusively one, without a second—except for the Buddha’s skillful means, which are not to be mentioned here.
He said: "If the bodhisattvas did not seek the vehicle, for what reason would they joyfully mount the vehicle?

From the passage beginning "I tell you, Śāriputra, you and all such people," the fourth section consists of fifteen and a half verses, which praise the fourth point: the analogy of the non-falsity [of the Buddha's teaching].
The preceding section on "correspondence" had two parts: first, two analogies were presented, followed by their correspondence to reality;
now, this section merely provides a verse summary of the correspondence to reality, which consists of two parts:
the first three and a half lines directly summarize the chapter heading on correspondence to reality; [the remainder follows].

Next, from "If there is a bodhisattva" onwards, the second section consists of twelve verses which provide a combined explanation of the non-futility [of the Buddha's teaching]; Śāriputra offers a simile for how this accords with his own original intention and is not in vain.

The father originally intended to enable his sons to escape the calamity, and thus he provided the three carts; since they have already been delivered from the danger—even though he did not give them the small carts—he has not contradicted his original intention, and therefore it was not in vain.

The Buddha’s parable clarifies that his teaching is not in vain; it reveals that the Buddha’s original intent was precisely to preach the One Vehicle. However, because beings in the five turbidities were unwilling to believe and accept it, he preached the Three Vehicles. Once the obstacles of the turbidities are removed, he returns to preaching the One Great Vehicle, which accords with his fundamental intention.
Regarding the first section, it is divided into three parts.

First, one line establishes the relationship between father and son; it clarifies that the fundamental intention was to grant the Great [Vehicle] to them, as the text says, "All are my sons," and by principle, they should equally receive the Great [Vehicle].

Next, from "You all" onwards, the second section consists of one verse clarifying that the intention for teaching the three vehicles is to eliminate obstacles; thus it says, "You all have been burned by manifold sufferings throughout many eons."

Next, from "Although I previously... onwards is the third section, consisting of one and a half lines. Since the obstacles have already been removed, he returns to fulfilling his original intention by bestowing the Mahāyāna Dharma; thus it says, "What I must now do is solely the wisdom of the Buddha."
From "If there are bodhisattvas" below, the second section consists of twelve lines of verse that provide a combined explanation, returning to explain the previous three points.
The first two verses explain the principle that since all are equally his children, they should logically be treated with equality.
Next, from "If a person of small wisdom" below, the second part consists of seven verses explaining that because [beings] are unable to receive [the full teaching], the Three Vehicles were taught.
Next, following the passage beginning with "In reality, however," is the third section, which consists of three verses explaining how, if one is capable, one should return the great [gift].

Now, regarding the first two lines: "If there is a bodhisattva" refers to those sentient beings transformed through the expedient means of the Three Vehicles; they were all Buddha-sons with whom [the Buddha] formed karmic connections in the past, and they all equally possess the *tathatā* (suchness) Buddha-nature. Therefore, it is said that they are all bodhisattvas.

From "If a person of small wisdom" onwards is the second section; these seven lines clarify that those of small wisdom have heavy obstacles and do not immediately believe and accept [the teaching], and thus, as a skillful means, the three [vehicles] are opened to guide and lead those of small wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "preaching the Truth of Suffering": among the three vehicles, the śrāvaka is the least; furthermore, the Truth of Suffering serves as their primary gateway.

Regarding the phrase "the minds of sentient beings rejoice": they rejoice because it accords with their original habitual tendencies. Having originally loathed birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and sought nirvāṇa for themselves, now hearing the teaching on transcendence immediately accords with their past habits, and thus they feel great joy.
Herein, the focus is on the four truths with effort (*sābhisamskāra*).
Regarding the phrase "merely departing from delusion": ignorance (*avidyā*) is already unreal; since the pervasive afflictions arise in dependence upon ignorance, they are termed "delusions.

The four truths with effort merely eliminate these afflictions, which is called "liberation" (*vimukti*). However, because one is liberated from the *paricchinna* (segmented) realm but not yet liberated from the *pariṇāma* (transformative) realm, it is not yet sovereign (*vaśitā*).

From "In reality, [he] has not yet attained" below, the third section consists of three verses which explain that since the obstacles have been removed and the faculties have become sharp, he is able to fulfill his original aspiration by bestowing the Mahāyāna Dharma upon him.

The Buddha originally intended to grant liberation to all; now that you have merely severed the bonds of分段 (pudgala-bheda), this is not yet Great Nirvana. Because you have not yet attained everything, it ultimately does not accord with my original intention; therefore, he says, "It is not my wish to let you reach extinction."
Now, by causing them to attain the Unsurpassed Way and enter Great Nirvana, this is the ultimate fulfillment of the Buddha’s original intention.

All liberation is precisely the unconditioned Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), and the Unsurpassed Way is precisely the unconditioned Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). By means of these two truths, one destroys the unconditioned Truths of Suffering and Origination. Previously, I wished to preach this, but these sentient beings were not yet capable; now that their obstructions have been removed, I preach it once again.
The Buddha is the Dharma King; having attained mastery over both provisional and ultimate teachings, he opens up the three to reveal the one reality—how could there be any falsehood?
The passage beginning with "O Śāriputra, this Dharma-seal of mine" consists of six sections and fifteen lines of verse, which exhort [the reader] to believe and circulate [this teaching].

"Faith" refers to believing whether the Buddha has spoken or not; "exhortation" refers to encouraging what is penetrable or what is impenetrable. Because these two meanings exist, they are called "exhortation and faith.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the presentation of the two chapters; second, the explanation.
Regarding the first line, which marks what was spoken and what was not spoken: the Tathāgata spoke this Dharma-seal for the sake of benefiting the world;
as for what was not spoken, it was because for more than forty years it was not yet the time to speak it, and because the five thousand [monks] had not yet departed, he therefore did not speak it.

Next, regarding the second half of the line "In whatever direction one travels," which marks the chapter on what may or may not be communicated: do not propagate [the teaching] recklessly. If one were to force an evil person to speak [of it], they would fall into suffering; if one were not to speak of it to a good person, they would be misled and lose their happiness. If, out of great compassion, one pities the evil, one should not communicate it; if, out of great kindness, one regards the good, one should communicate it. This is called the chapter marking what may or may not be communicated.
From the phrase "If there are those who hear," this is the second [section], the explanation, which is further divided into two parts:
first, eight lines explaining what can be spoken and what cannot be spoken;
second, fifty and a half lines explaining what is penetrable and what is impenetrable.
Now, the first eight lines clarify the manner in which the Tathāgata benefits the world.
Generally speaking, they concern his benefit across the three periods of time; specifically, they concern his leading the followers of the two vehicles into faith.
"Avaivartika" (non-retrogressive) refers to observing present benefit; "having previously seen" refers to speaking based on observing past goodness.

"Those who believe in you and me" refers to speaking based on observing future goodness; the meaning is as stated in the subsequent text: "If one has deep faith and understanding, they shall see the Buddha eternally dwelling on Vulture Peak."

This single practice of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* concludes what has preceded and opens what follows. The Tathāgata, having observed and known the benefits for [beings] across the three periods of time, therefore preaches it; however, he does not preach it to those of shallow wisdom who do not understand.
This is the commentary on the chapter concerning “The Tathāgata’s Speaking and Not Speaking.

From the section beginning with “Arrogance and Laziness” downward, it explains the chapter on whether practitioners are capable or incapable [of receiving the teaching]. This section is further divided into two parts; the first thirty-six and a half lines clarify that if one employs the gate of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one must not preach to those who would commit evil. First, it cites the various forms of evil, showing that such persons will inevitably give rise to malicious slander and incur evil retributions; therefore, one must not preach to them out of great compassion.
Regarding the phrase "severing the Buddha-seed in the world": the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* takes afflictions (*kleśa*) as the Tathāgata-seed, which refers to the nature of the objective realm;

the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* takes the study of all-aspect wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) through prajñā as the Buddha-seed, which refers to the nature of the contributing cause (*upādāna-hetu*);
and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* takes the principle of the mind-nature’s non-interruption as the Buddha-seed, which refers to the nature of the primary cause (*hetu-hetu*).

This sutra clarifies that even minor wholesome deeds lead to Buddhahood; this takes the causal condition as the seed of a Buddha. If one does not believe that minor wholesome deeds lead to Buddhahood, one severs the worldly seed of the Buddhas.

The nineteen lines beginning with "If there are those of sharp faculties" explain the application of the gate of great compassion when propagating the sutra; good persons should proclaim it for others so that they do not lose their joy.

As for the essentials of broad propagation, it consists in harmonizing the two gates so that each finds its proper place; this is true transmission. If they do not find their proper place, it is a false proclamation.
The text is divided into two parts:
the first seventeen lines describe five pairs and ten individual characteristics of virtuous people, which may be proclaimed and explained.
The final two lines summarize what should be explained.

First, the past and present form a pair: "sharp faculties" refers to the present, while "planting roots of goodness" refers to the past; "strong memory" refers to the present, while "seeing hundreds of thousands" refers to the past.
Second, the superior and inferior form a pair: "cultivating loving-kindness" is compassion for those below, while "reverence" is honoring those above.

Third, the pair of outer and inner: "Abandoning evil and befriending the good" is seeking externally; "Maintaining the precepts like a jewel" is guarding internally. Fourth, the pair of self-cultivation and transforming others: "Being upright and revering the Buddha" is self-cultivation; "Expounding the Dharma through parables" is transforming others. Fifth, the pair of beginning and end:

"Seeking the Dharma in the four directions" is the beginning of requesting instruction; "Receiving it upon one's head and practicing with single-minded devotion" is the end of taking refuge and reliance, and so forth.
The two lines beginning with "Tell Śāriputra" serve as a summary.

Although those of good faith are numerous, ten characteristics are briefly cited to demonstrate the method for the circulation [of this teaching], thereby clarifying the essential points regarding when the two gates of compassion and wisdom may or may not be communicated.

Commentary on the Chapter on Faith and Understanding: Regarding the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding," some say that there are three modes of faith and understanding, namely: initial transformation, subsequent transformation, and ultimate transformation. What was previously described as the "Great" is the initial transformation; turning away from the Great is the subsequent transformation; and the meeting of father and son is the ultimate transformation.

Furthermore, the wholesome deeds of humans and devas constitute the "initial stage"; teaching the Hīnayāna up to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitutes the "subsequent stage"; and attaining the prediction of enlightenment through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitutes the "ultimate stage.

Moreover, the initial teaching of the two vehicles constitutes the "initial stage"; the turning of the wheel of instruction constitutes the "subsequent stage"; and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitutes the "ultimate stage."
Furthermore, teaching through transformation is the "initial stage," traversing the Vaipulya sūtras is the "subsequent stage," and awakening to the One Vehicle is the "ultimate stage.

Moreover, preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the "initial stage," the constant teaching throughout the ten stages is the "subsequent stage," and reaching the diamond-like mind is the "ultimate stage."

Furthermore, regarding the *saṃnāha-saṃvara* (the armor of resolve): "one-way" (*ekayāna*) refers to the initial setting forth; "following along" refers to the intermediate stages; and "attaining Buddhahood" refers to the ultimate consummation.

I privately remark that these various interpretations are redundant—like jade fragments, they are not the true jewel. For "one-way" is not the original intent, while the "ultimate" is the final goal. To say that teaching the human and celestial realms or the two vehicles constitutes "one-way" may well be the case as not being the original intent; however, when the Great Vehicle was taught in the past and now the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is taught, this is precisely the ultimate consummation—how then can it be called "one-way"?
If the *Lotus Sūtra* were ultimately a provisional teaching (*ekāntika*), and the cycle of humans and devas were ultimately a final realization, that would be a great perversion.
Furthermore, since the two vehicles are provisional, the grass hut must be demolished;
since the former "great" [teaching] was provisional, the binding of the jewel must also be undone.
If one [aspect] is broken while the other is not, then one is a provisional approach and the other is not a provisional approach.

Furthermore, if the ultimate reality (*atyanta*) of father and son meeting were itself the ultimate, then the prior ultimate would have already realized oneness, rendering the subsequent ultimate redundant;
if, however, it is through the subsequent ultimate that oneness is realized, then the prior ultimate is not the ultimate.
There are obstacles at every section, so none of them are used now.
Some say that this chapter is a "trace" (a provisional teaching). Why?
The Tathāgata attained enlightenment long ago; even the periods of cessation during the intervening time are merely traces.
In my private view, while this is indeed the case regarding the underlying principle (*artha*), it is not convenient when expressed in the literal text (*vyañjana*).
Why is this? Before the Buddha has yet spoken of the fundamental and the manifested, how can you suddenly presume to comprehend them?
If you had already realized the One before understanding the Three, then so be it—and so forth.

Now, regarding the explanation of this chapter: individuals possess faculties that are either sharp or dull, and afflictions that are either thick or thin; teachings employ both principles and analogies, and awakening occurs either early or late.

At the assembly before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, [the disciples] were like mung beans. As the text says: "The Tathāgata has been preaching the Dharma for a long time, and while I was seated there, my body grew weary and exhausted; I thought only of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and harbored not a single thought of delight in the Bodhisattva teachings."

"Initially, upon hearing the brief exposition, my attachments were shaken and doubts arose; later, hearing the extensive teaching, I was bewildered and remained unenlightened. Now, hearing these parables, I am filled with joy and exultation; faith has been awakened, understanding has arisen, doubt has departed, and the principle is clarified."

Joy is the world; the arising of faith is the person; the removal of doubt is the remedy; and the clarification of principle is the ultimate meaning. For these reasons, it is called the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding."

In receiving the teachings of both the Small and Great Vehicles, there are respective stages for initially transforming the ordinary into the sagely. However, in the Small Vehicle, those who practice through faith (*śraddhā-carita*) generate understanding from what they hear; when the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) arises and their faith becomes manifest, it is called "practice" (*caryā*).

Those who practice through the Dharma (*dharma-carita*) observe the phenomena sequentially; when the patience regarding suffering arises and their realization of the Dharma becomes manifest, it is called "practice."
If a practitioner by faith (*śraddhā-carita*) enters the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), they are renamed "one resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*);
if a practitioner by dharma (*dharma-carita*) enters the path of cultivation, they are renamed "one who has attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
By analogy with the Lesser Vehicle, this should also apply to the Greater Vehicle.

Those of medium capacity, upon hearing the exposition of parables, first shatter their doubts and enter the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) of the Mahāyāna; therefore, this is called "faith" (*śraddhā*). Subsequently, they enter the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) of the Mahāyāna; therefore, this is called "understanding" (*adhimukti*).
The text says: "This unsurpassed treasury of jewels is obtained spontaneously without seeking; today we are truly śrāvakas.
Because the sound of the Buddha-way causes all to hear, and by hearing the Perfect Teaching they enter the Perfect Stage, it is therefore named the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding."

Regarding the "Original and the Traces": the four great disciples have long entered the Mahāyāna and achieved the Buddha-dharma; yet, as traces, they lead those of medium capacity by demonstrating initial faith and understanding. Therefore, it is named the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding."
This is the section on the realization of understanding; it closely summarizes the "Burning House" chapter and distantly summarizes the "Expedient Means" chapter.
The text consists of two parts:
first, the narrator describes their joy; second, they address the Buddha to speak for themselves.
First the inner mind is described, followed by outward reverence.
Subhūti alone is called "Life of Wisdom" (*prajñājīvita*).

Regarding the three who are called "Great" (*mahā*): in general discourse, they are all great and all possess wisdom; in specific discourse, Subhūti takes the wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness as his life—this refers to his practice.

Among all those with wisdom, the Buddha’s wisdom is foremost; the Buddha commanded him to propagate the teachings of the *Prajñā[pāramitā]*. Because he was so commanded by one possessed of wisdom, he is called "Wisdom-Life" (*prajñājīvita*).
The three disciples received a limited mandate and did not take emptiness as the core of their practice;
this is the provisional teaching (*yōkyō*). Regarding "Mahā," it is as previously explained, etc.

As for the cause of attaining joy, it is heard from afar that the Dharma was taught in five sections concerning skillful means (*upāya*); the sūtra compiler merely records two types: hearing the rare Dharma and hearing the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*). Alternatively, hearing the rare Dharma may be described as comprising four sections, with seeing the reception of the prediction being the fifth section.
To hear and see such things as have never occurred before is the cause for one’s joy.

Regarding the phrase "giving rise to a rare and marvelous mind," this describes how, upon hearing the fourfold parables just recounted, a rare and marvelous mind is produced; because the mind is produced, it is called "faith" (*śraddhā*). Because of this faith, one enters [the path], entering the stage of joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*); this is precisely the meaning of the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding."
Regarding "rising from one's seat," this describes external reverence as stated in the text.
Taking Śāriputra as an example, he likewise should have understood through the three karmas (of body, speech, and mind), which can be understood by analogy with what precedes.
From "He addressed the Buddha" onwards, he personally recounts his experience; the text is divided into two parts:
first, the prose section and seventy-three and a half verses, which properly recount his attainment of understanding;
second, thirteen verses, which praise the profundity of the Buddha’s grace.
This interpretation is derived from the Buddha; therefore, it is first presented and subsequently praised.
The prose section further consists of two parts:
first, a brief exposition by way of the Dharma; second, an extensive exposition by way of analogy.
Briefly, there are two parts:
the explanation of the Dharma and a brief citation of analogies.
The explanation of the Dharma also consists of two parts:
First, it clarifies that because one has previously received the three [vehicles], there is no seeking; second, it clarifies that because one now realizes the one, it is spontaneously attained.
Within the section on "no seeking," there is both a heading and an explanation.
The heading consists of three parts:
First, because he occupies the headship of the monastic community; second, because his secular age is advanced; and third, because of his realization.

Regarding the first point, as my years of ordination (*dharma-varṣa*) are already high, those who have recently entered the study take me as their model. If I were suddenly to change my path and alter my course, abandoning the small for the great, I would be resented by those who come after; thus, I seek it not in order to firmly protect them.

Second, my secular age has already advanced; had I been a bodhisattva, I would have devoted myself solely to the Great Way to extensively deliver sentient beings. Now that I am decrepit and old, I am incapable of such tasks, and for this reason I do not seek it.

Third, having already attained the unconditioned state of parinirvāṇa, they are unable to give rise to the great mind; just as lotuses do not grow on high plateaus or dry land, their knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising is already established, and they have nothing further upon which to rely or seek.

Why is this? The three "non-seekings" are explained out of sequence in the text: first, the non-seeking of attaining *nirvāṇa* is explained; next, the non-seeking of advanced age is explained, which simultaneously includes [the non-seeking of] being the head of the Saṃgha; or it may refer to the fact that because he had long been preaching the Dharma in the past, his mind no longer found delight in it.

The monk Faju (釋法住) was the head of the monastic community; he did not seek [the position], yet having said he was present in the assembly, he further remarked that his years were advanced—thus we know he was the head of the monks.
The passage regarding the monk Faju is as written in the text.

From the words "We now, before the Buddha... onwards, he sets forth the reason for attaining understanding: because he had long heard the five chapters briefly expound and extensively open the three vehicles to reveal the single reality, he therefore felt joy and gratitude.

Regarding the phrase "attaining great and wholesome benefit," this correctly describes the attainment of understanding; it refers to attaining awakening upon hearing these four rare parables, which constitutes the wholesome benefit of such awakening.

From "Immeasurable Treasures" downwards, the second section is a brief illustration, which serves as a metaphor for how that which was not sought in the past is now spontaneously obtained—the rare Dharma-treasure.

From "World-Honored One, we wish to speak by way of a parable" onwards is the extensive explanation of understanding; it contains both the opening of the parable and its application to the teaching. Before opening the parable, [the interlocutors] first inquire and express their intent, and so forth.
There are five parables:

first, from "Abandoning his father and fleeing" downward, it is called the Parable of Father and Son Losing Sight of Each Other; this closely summarizes the general parable of the Burning House and distantly summarizes the brief verse on the Expedient Means.

Second, from "The impoverished son working for hire" downward, it is called the Parable of Father and Son Meeting; this closely summarizes the scene of seeing the fire in the Burning House and distantly summarizes my observation with the Buddha-eye as described in the Expedient Means.

3. From "He immediately dispatched attendants to pursue and bring him back" onwards is called the Parable of the Pursuit and Enticement; it closely leads to the abandonment of the low stools and the provision of the carts within the burning house, and distantly leads to the concealment of the Great [Vehicle] and the bestowing of the Small [Vehicle] as skillful means;

4. From "After this period, their hearts came to trust one another" onwards is the Parable of Fully Understanding the Family Business; this does not lead to the aforementioned near and distant [meanings], but rather follows up on the intent of the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras) that rebuke and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* that transform the teaching;

5. From "After a short while more, the father knew his son's intention" onwards is called the Parable of Entrusting the Family Business; it closely leads to the granting of the single great cart within the burning house, and distantly leads to the Dharma-exposition’s directness of abandoning skillful means.
Furthermore, the fourth and fifth [analogies] are combined into a single illustration of entrustment, the meaning of which will be further clarified below.
Previously, the Western Amitābha Buddha was identified with the elder; however, that is not adopted here.

In the Western [tradition], the Buddhas are distinct and their conditions differ. Because the Buddhas are distinct, the principle of concealment and manifestation is not established; because the conditions differ, the analogy of son and father is not established.
Furthermore, this scripture contains no such intent from beginning to end; to force an interpretation here is to close one's eyes and engage in speculative excavation.

Now, relying on the text to elucidate the meaning: if one explains the "poor son," one takes the *bāla-akṣara* (half-syllable) Dharma of those of the Two Vehicles to interpret the text; if one explains the "elder," one takes the *paripūrṇa-akṣara* (full-syllable) Dharma-gate of Vairocana Buddha to interpret the text.

Why is this? Within the house, the elder removes his jeweled necklace and puts on soiled garments; though the clothing and ornaments differ, the person remains one and the same. This is analogous to Vairocana Buddha, who conceals his immeasurable divine virtues to manifest as a sixteen-foot golden radiance, holding a dung-bowl and establishing the teachings of the Three Vehicles. Although there is a distinction between concealment and manifestation, how does this concern a difference in essence? If one does not even know that Vairocana’s appearance changes when he puts on or takes off his robes while nearby, how could one ever suspect a transformation when Amitābha is far away? And so forth.
The analogy of the father and son losing one another is further explained in four parts:
